title: David Dhawan Directed His Last Scene. His Son Was Standing Right in Front of the Camera.
excerpt: Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai crosses ₹60 crore worldwide. But for everyone who grew up on Coolie No. 1 and Hero No. 1, the number that matters is this: 45 films. Zero more.
body:
There is a moment during the promotions of Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai where David Dhawan says something so quietly it almost gets lost in the noise of the press junket. "I don't think I should do more," he tells the room. "This might be my last film. After this, I'll just be Varun's father."

https://youtube.com/watch?v=rFOdIv1jwhc

Six words. That's all it took to close a four-decade chapter of Indian cinema.

The Last Reel

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai released on June 5 and has since crossed ₹60 crore worldwide — ₹36.85 crore net in India through its first week, with another ₹11.85 crore from overseas markets. Against a reported budget of ₹50-55 crore, the film is heading toward a modest theatrical profit. Not a blockbuster. Not a disaster. Somewhere in between — which, if you think about it, is a perfectly David Dhawan way to go out: not with a bang or a whimper, but with a shrug and a punchline.

!David Dhawan — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

**"Filmfare gave it 3 out of 5, calling it "pure, unabashed farce" and a "time capsule from the era when he and Govinda ruled the box office."

That era."**

The film stars Varun Dhawan, Mrunal Thakur, and Pooja Hegde in a story about a marriage that falls apart over family planning and a husband who finds new chaos abroad. Shot across Mumbai, Goa, Rishikesh, and Edinburgh, it's vintage David Dhawan — mistaken identities, fake relatives, unexpected pregnancies, and the kind of situational comedy that doesn't ask you to think, just to laugh. Filmfare gave it 3 out of 5, calling it "pure, unabashed farce" and a "time capsule from the era when he and Govinda ruled the box office."

That era. Let's talk about that era.

The Man Who Made India Laugh

If you were an Indian kid in the 1990s — whether in Mumbai, Delhi, or a living room in New Jersey where your parents rented VHS tapes from the local Indian grocery store — David Dhawan was inescapable. Coolie No. 1. Hero No. 1. Bade Miyan Chote Miyan. Saajan Chale Sasural. Judwaa. He didn't make cinema. He made a mood. He made the kind of films where Govinda could wear a purple shirt and orange pants and somehow look like the coolest man alive, where every plot twist was absurd and every audience member was in on the joke.

He directed 45 films across his career. Seventeen of them featured Govinda — a partnership so reliable that it essentially invented a genre. David Dhawan comedies weren't comedies in the Hrishikesh Mukherjee sense; they were sugar rushes, engineered for pure dopamine. And for an entire generation of NRIs, they were the soundtrack to Sunday afternoons, to road trips where the car DVD player cycled through Biwi No. 1 and Dulhan Hum Le Jayenge until the disc scratched.

!The Last Reel — Photo: Wikimedia Commons

Father and Son, One Last Time

Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai marks the fourth collaboration between David Dhawan and Varun — after Main Tera Hero, Judwaa 2, and Coolie No. 1 (the 2020 remake). The dynamic has always been specific: David treats Varun like any other actor on set. "When I'm behind the camera, he's not my son, he is an actor," he has said. "I just need the result."

But off-camera, there's a tenderness that leaks through. Varun has spoken about watching his father's health struggles and wanting him to rest. David, in turn, has deflected with the kind of gruff affection that his films specialise in — the father who expresses love through exasperation.

Karan Johar, who attended a special celebration for David Dhawan ahead of the release, couldn't hold it together. "Yesterday, when I went to Davidji's celebration, he told me this was going to be his last film," Karan wrote on Instagram. "I had a bittersweet reaction in my heart. Here's a filmmaker who is responsible for creating an entire genre of films. A DAVID DHAWAN film spells entertainment."

Where to Watch

For diaspora audiences in the US, UK, and Canada, Hai Jawani Toh Ishq Hona Hai is currently running in select theatres through Tips Films' international distribution. No OTT release date has been announced yet — so if you want to catch David Dhawan's final film on the big screen, this is your window.

Whether you think the film is a masterpiece or a throwback you've outgrown, here's what's not up for debate: the man behind the camera gave us something irreplaceable. He made a country of a billion people laugh at the same jokes at the same time. And he chose to walk away on his own terms, with his son in front of the lens and a comedy playing in the background.

Some exits are just right.
